body.text: In brief

• Bulgaria's President Iliana Iotova narrowly led the first round of presidential elections on Monday, exit polls showed, in a vote held amid security concerns following a series of drone attacks on ships in the Black Sea. Iotova, who favours dialogue with Russia and opposes military aid to Ukraine, scored between 35 and 36.5 per cent of the vote, according to three polls. She will face Andrey Gyurov, a banker and former caretaker prime minister backed by the pro-Western opposition who came second with between 32.2 and 32.5 per cent, in the 1 November runoff. The result was closer than expected, with surveys ahead of the vote predicting a comfortable win for Iotova. Turnout was only around 20 per cent, according to the polls. After casting her vote, Iotova said she wanted to address "the dire issue of poverty" in the EU's poorest member state, "alongside inequalities and regional disparities". "I believe that there must be peace, stability, and security," added the 62-year-old, who has made the war in Ukraine a central theme of her campaign, promising to be a "president of peace". Gyurov meanwhile said he wanted "a Bulgaria that looks forward, a country that is European, free, and proud... and where the state works as it should". Ship attacks Four vessels were struck off Bulgaria's coast this month, leaving 21 people missing, in suspected spillover from the Russia-Ukraine war. While Prime Minister Rumen Radev said the attacks appeared to serve Russian interests and summoned the Russian ambassador, his government insists there is so far no evidence directly linking Russia to them. Iotova took over this year as president of Bulgaria, a European Union and NATO member state, when Radev stepped down to run in parliamentary elections. If successful in the runoff, she would become the first woman ever elected president in the country of 6.4 million people. A win for Iotova would be a boost for Radev, who has also called for dialogue with Russia. A former journalist and member of the European Parliament, Iotova was elected vice-president alongside Radev in 2016 and 2021. Without questioning Bulgaria's membership of the EU or NATO, she opposes military aid to Ukraine and advocates negotiations. Gyurov, 50, has sharply criticised Radev's foreign policy and is a strong supporter of Bulgaria's Euro-Atlantic ties. At his final campaign rally in Plovdiv on Wednesday, Gyurov said he wanted Bulgaria to be "a reliable ally within NATO, defending its interests through solid preparedness, strong diplomacy and clear positions". 'Unconvincing response' Parvan Simeonov, founder of polling institute Myara, said Iotova "did not step out of her presidential role" during the campaign, "which prevented her from engaging in sharper debate". He added that the low turnout showed "that we don't have a problem with the polls, but with the very functioning of democracy". Casting his vote earlier, Radev blamed the low turnout on the "significant lead between the first and second according to surveys, which gives reassurance in one camp and perhaps a sense of doom in the other". Historically close to Russia, Bulgaria remains deeply divided over its relationship with Russia. Twenty-seven pairs of candidates for president and vice-president were competing in the first round, nearly half of them openly pro-Kremlin. Teodor Slavev, a political analyst and programme director at the Bulgarian Institute for Legal Initiatives, told the Agence France-Presse news agency the results were "a resounding electoral slap in the face for Rumen Radev's administration and their inability to address people's problems". He also said voters were giving their verdict on "Iotova's unconvincing response regarding Russian threats in the Black Sea". <hr></hr>For the latest from SBS News, download our app and subscribe to our newsletter.
• Security fears and the war in Ukraine are shaping the election debate.

Bulgaria's President Iliana Iotova narrowly led the first round of presidential elections on Monday, exit polls showed, in a vote held amid security concerns following a series of drone attacks on ships in the Black Sea.
Iotova, who favours dialogue with Russia and opposes military aid to Ukraine, scored between 35 and 36.5 per cent of the vote, according to three polls.
She will face Andrey Gyurov, a banker and former caretaker prime minister backed by the pro-Western opposition who came second with between 32.2 and 32.5 per cent, in the 1 November runoff.
The result was closer than expected, with surveys ahead of the vote predicting a comfortable win for Iotova.
Turnout was only around 20 per cent, according to the polls.
After casting her vote, Iotova said she wanted to address "the dire issue of poverty" in the EU's poorest member state, "alongside inequalities and regional disparities".
"I believe that there must be peace, stability, and security," added the 62-year-old, who has made the war in Ukraine a central theme of her campaign, promising to be a "president of peace".
Gyurov meanwhile said he wanted "a Bulgaria that looks forward, a country that is European, free, and proud... and where the state works as it should".
Ship attacks
Four vessels were struck off Bulgaria's coast this month, leaving 21 people missing, in suspected spillover from the Russia-Ukraine war.

While Prime Minister Rumen Radev said the attacks appeared to serve Russian interests and summoned the Russian ambassador, his government insists there is so far no evidence directly linking Russia to them.
Iotova took over this year as president of Bulgaria, a European Union and NATO member state, when Radev stepped down to run in parliamentary elections.
If successful in the runoff, she would become the first woman ever elected president in the country of 6.4 million people.
A win for Iotova would be a boost for Radev, who has also called for dialogue with Russia.
A former journalist and member of the European Parliament, Iotova was elected vice-president alongside Radev in 2016 and 2021.
Without questioning Bulgaria's membership of the EU or NATO, she opposes military aid to Ukraine and advocates negotiations.
Gyurov, 50, has sharply criticised Radev's foreign policy and is a strong supporter of Bulgaria's Euro-Atlantic ties.

At his final campaign rally in Plovdiv on Wednesday, Gyurov said he wanted Bulgaria to be "a reliable ally within NATO, defending its interests through solid preparedness, strong diplomacy and clear positions".
'Unconvincing response'
Parvan Simeonov, founder of polling institute Myara, said Iotova "did not step out of her presidential role" during the campaign, "which prevented her from engaging in sharper debate".
He added that the low turnout showed "that we don't have a problem with the polls, but with the very functioning of democracy".

Casting his vote earlier, Radev blamed the low turnout on the "significant lead between the first and second according to surveys, which gives reassurance in one camp and perhaps a sense of doom in the other".
Historically close to Russia, Bulgaria remains deeply divided over its relationship with Russia.
Twenty-seven pairs of candidates for president and vice-president were competing in the first round, nearly half of them openly pro-Kremlin.

Teodor Slavev, a political analyst and programme director at the Bulgarian Institute for Legal Initiatives, told the Agence France-Presse news agency the results were "a resounding electoral slap in the face for Rumen Radev's administration and their inability to address people's problems".
He also said voters were giving their verdict on "Iotova's unconvincing response regarding Russian threats in the Black Sea".
